title: Advanced Grammar — Unit 1 — Variant 2
topics: Verbs with state and action meanings

questions.question: I ______ these figures to be accurate; they were checked independently on two occasions.
questions.explanation: Believe is a state verb expressing an opinion, so the present simple is used.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: am believing: not normally used in the continuous; believes: wrong with I; have been believing: continuous form is unsuitable here.
questions.tip: Compare: I believe he is right.

questions.question: The programme ______ of six taught modules and a substantial research project.
questions.explanation: Consist of describes the permanent composition of something and is used in the simple form.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: is consisting and has been consisting: consist of is not normally continuous; consist: wrong with the singular subject programme.
questions.tip: Be made up of and comprise are similar alternatives.

questions.question: To anyone who grew up in the eighties, the opening track ______ remarkably familiar.
questions.explanation: Sound meaning give an impression is a state verb; the track has a general characteristic.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: is sounding: unsuitable for this general impression; sound: wrong subject-verb agreement; has been sounding: unsuitable continuous form.
questions.tip: The proposal sounds sensible.

questions.question: The twins usually dread visitors, but they ______ having their cousins to stay this week.
questions.explanation: The contrast with usually and the temporary period this week supports the present continuous.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: love: does not express the temporary contrast as intended; loves: wrong with they; have been loving: unnatural here.
questions.tip: Some verbs such as love can take continuous forms for temporary or emphatic situations.

questions.question: As a rule the gallery attracts an older audience, but this season it ______ a noticeably younger crowd.
questions.explanation: As a rule describes the usual situation; this season describes a temporary change.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: attracts: misses the contrast; attract: wrong with it; has been attracted: passive and changes the meaning.
questions.tip: Usual pattern: present simple; temporary trend: present continuous.

questions.question: Which of the following sentences is incorrect?

options.text: The proposal sounds perfectly sensible to me.
She's staying at a hotel until the flat is ready.
The kit consists of ten precision tools.
I'm doubting his account of what happened.

questions.explanation: Doubt is normally a state verb and is not usually used in the present continuous in this meaning.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: The other sentences are acceptable: sounds gives an impression; is staying describes a temporary arrangement; consists describes composition.
questions.tip: Use: I doubt his account.

questions.question: She rarely does theatre work, but she ______ in a musical for the next six weeks.
questions.explanation: Appear meaning perform or take part is an action; the limited future period supports the present continuous.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: appears: suggests a regular occurrence; appear: wrong with she; has been appearing: does not fit the stated upcoming period.
questions.tip: Appear can mean seem (state) or perform (action).

questions.question: I ______ that the meeting will be relatively short, given how little there is on the agenda.
questions.explanation: Expect in a that-clause means suppose or think, so the present simple is natural.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: am expecting: usually means waiting for something here; expects: wrong with I; have been expecting: unnatural for this opinion.
questions.tip: I expect that it will be short.

questions.question: Don't go out just yet - we ______ visitors at any moment.
questions.explanation: Expect means wait for or anticipate someone's arrival; this is a current situation.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: expect: less suitable for the immediate arrangement; expects: wrong with we; have been expecting: unnecessary perfect continuous form.
questions.tip: We're expecting visitors.

questions.question: Please stay still for a moment - the doctor ______ your arm to see where the pain is.
questions.explanation: Feel means touch or examine with the hand here, describing an action happening now.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: feels: simple form does not express the action in progress; feel: wrong agreement; has been feeling: does not fit the immediate instruction.
questions.tip: Compare: I feel we should wait / The doctor is feeling your arm.

questions.question: I ______ strongly that we should postpone the decision until the spring.
questions.explanation: Feel means hold an opinion here, so the present simple is used.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: am feeling: usually describes a temporary physical or emotional condition; feels: wrong with I; have been feeling: unsuitable for this opinion.
questions.tip: I feel that we should wait.

questions.question: You ______ things - nobody in this office said anything of the sort.
questions.explanation: The context refers to something the listener is currently imagining incorrectly; the continuous form emphasizes the ongoing mental activity.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: imagine: less suited to the immediate accusation; imagines: wrong with you; have been imagining: unnecessarily emphasizes duration.
questions.tip: Compare: I imagine it will rain (suppose) with You're imagining things.

questions.question: The proposal ______ promising on paper, but the costings are completely unrealistic.
questions.explanation: Look means seem or give an impression here, so the present simple is used.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: is looking: not the normal form for this general impression; look: wrong with the singular subject; has been looking: unsuitable.
questions.tip: The plan looks promising.

questions.question: After the refurbishment, the main hall ______ eighteen metres by twelve.
questions.explanation: Measure means have particular dimensions here; this is a characteristic, so use the present simple.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: is measuring and has been measuring: describe an act of measuring; measure: wrong with the singular subject.
questions.tip: The room measures five metres by four.

questions.question: I ______ Bukhara one of the most beautiful cities I have ever visited.
questions.explanation: Find means consider or judge something to be a certain way; this is a general evaluation.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: am finding: suggests a developing opinion; finds: wrong with I; have been finding: unnatural here.
questions.tip: Find + object + adjective is common: I find it useful.

questions.question: I ______ the new software easier and easier now that I use it every single day.
questions.explanation: Easier and easier shows a changing evaluation developing over time, so the present continuous is appropriate.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: find: does not highlight the developing change; finds: wrong with I; have been found: passive and incorrect in meaning.
questions.tip: Compare: I find it difficult / I'm finding it easier.

questions.question: At last I ______ why she reacted the way she did at the meeting.
questions.explanation: Understand is normally a state verb. At last indicates that the speaker now has the understanding.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: am understanding and have been understanding: not normally used in this sense; understands: wrong with I.
questions.tip: A natural alternative is I'm beginning to understand.

questions.question: I ______ this is the most workable solution currently available to us.
questions.explanation: Think means hold an opinion here, so the present simple is used.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: am thinking: describes considering or deliberating; thinks: wrong with I; have been thinking: emphasizes a process rather than the stated opinion.
questions.tip: I think you're right / I'm thinking about it.

questions.question: We ______ of relocating the office to a smaller site next year.
questions.explanation: Think of + -ing means consider or plan; this is an ongoing consideration.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: think: does not express the current developing plan as clearly; thinks: wrong with we; have been thought: passive and incorrect.
questions.tip: Be thinking of + -ing often introduces a possible plan.

questions.question: The report ______ that the existing system is no longer safe to operate.
questions.explanation: In academic style, concludes that introduces the conclusion stated by a report.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: is concluding and has been concluding: unnatural for this reporting function; conclude: wrong with the singular subject.
questions.tip: The report concludes / argues / suggests that...

questions.question: I ______ that the money will be back in your account by Friday afternoon.
questions.explanation: Promise is used in the present simple as a performative: saying it makes the promise.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: am promising: not the usual affirmative performative form; promises: wrong with I; have been promising: suggests repeated promises.
questions.tip: I promise to look into it.

questions.question: I ______ that I was completely wrong about the dates in my last email.
questions.explanation: Admit is used in the present simple to perform the act of acknowledging something.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: am admitting: presents it as an ongoing process; admits: wrong with I; have been admitting: suggests repeated admissions.
questions.tip: I admit I was wrong.

questions.question: On behalf of the committee, we ______ you for all your help with the conference.
questions.explanation: The present simple is the standard formal performative for expressing thanks.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: are thanking: unnatural for this formal statement; thanks: wrong with we; have been thanking: suggests repeated action.
questions.tip: Thank somebody for something.

questions.question: We ______ receipt of your application and will respond within ten working days.
questions.explanation: Acknowledge receipt is a fixed formal expression confirming that something has been received.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: are acknowledging: less suitable for the formal performative; acknowledges: wrong with we; have been acknowledging: suggests repetition.
questions.tip: We acknowledge receipt of...

questions.question: I ______ to sign anything that I haven't had time to read properly.
questions.explanation: The present simple expresses a firm refusal in this statement.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: am refusing: emphasizes an ongoing or temporary stance; refuses: wrong with I; have been refusing: suggests repeated refusals.
questions.tip: I refuse to sign it.

questions.question: School regulations ______ students to leave the premises before the final bell.
questions.explanation: Forbid is used in the present simple to state a rule; regulations is plural.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: are forbidding and have been forbidding: unsuitable continuous forms for a standing rule; forbids: wrong agreement.
questions.tip: Forbid somebody to do something.

questions.question: The report ______ that energy prices will rise sharply over the next decade.
questions.explanation: Predicts that is a standard present-simple reporting structure for a report's content.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: is predicting and has been predicting: less natural for a statement of the report's conclusion; predict: wrong with the singular subject.
questions.tip: The report predicts / estimates / warns that...

questions.question: Which sentence would NOT normally be used?

options.text: I'm not promising anything at this stage.
I'm promising to look into it.
I don't promise anything at this stage.
I promise to look into it personally.

questions.explanation: An affirmative performative promise is normally expressed with the present simple, not the present continuous.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: The other options are possible: both simple and continuous can occur in negative promises; I promise is the standard affirmative performative.
questions.tip: Affirmative performative: I promise. Negative: I don't promise / I'm not promising.

questions.question: I ______ confess that our meeting had completely slipped my mind.
questions.explanation: Must is a modal verb followed by the base form confess. I must confess is a common expression introducing an admission.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: am, will be, and have been cannot be followed by the bare infinitive confess in these structures.
questions.tip: Modal + base verb: must confess.

questions.question: The regulations ______ candidates to use a monolingual dictionary in this particular paper.
questions.explanation: Permit is used in the present simple to state what the regulations allow; regulations is plural.
questions.whyOthersAreIncorrect: are permitting and have been permitting: unsuitable for a standing rule; permits: wrong agreement.
questions.tip: Permit somebody to do something; compare forbid somebody to do something.
